prototype_questions.question: Which active-leader fence and Redis epoch-install protocol prevents a stale gate process from mutating state or issuing accepted permits across PostgreSQL lease loss and delayed Redis writes?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted service has separate PostgreSQL latch and Redis state stores. The local probe tested row-lock serialization and Redis stale-epoch rejection separately, but not delayed writes, lease loss, split brain, or permit issuance through one service protocol. Compare candidates with deterministic failure injection before selecting the implementation contract.
decision_criteria: stale leader cannot mutate Redis after a higher epoch is installed
no permit issuance when owner, lease, lock, or epoch is uncertain
bounded recovery when a delayed old-epoch command lands before installation
durable monotonic epoch behavior across process restart and provider failover
bounded lock duration and simple operational recovery
lost PostgreSQL finalization and uncertain WAITAOF responses remain inhibited until provider evidence establishes the exact durable result
coordinated PostgreSQL and Redis restore cannot admit from a mutually consistent stale snapshot

candidates.approach: Use a PostgreSQL owner/epoch row lock with server-time lease validation across each bounded Redis mutation or permit issue, install the leader epoch in Redis with a monotonic Lua compare-and-set, and wait for the configured fsync threshold before serving.

Use a PostgreSQL transaction-scoped advisory lock plus a durable owner/epoch row compare-and-set, with the same monotonic Redis epoch installation and fsync barrier; deny work whenever either PostgreSQL signal is uncertain.

prototype_questions.question: How can command retries remain idempotent after one-year actor-audit deletion without retaining actor identity or operator reason indefinitely?
prototype_questions.rationale: PAUSE and RESUME command IDs must not produce duplicate transitions or become reusable with different requests. The accepted audit horizon is one year, so the persistent command-result/deduplication record needs a separate retention and deletion design. Prototype the smallest privacy-preserving option and measure storage/restore behavior.
decision_criteria: same command never advances generation twice
changed-request reuse is rejected after audit expiry
actor identity and operator reason are deleted on the accepted one-year horizon
minimal retained data and explainable backup/export deletion
recovery remains fail-closed after Redis or PostgreSQL restore
every authenticated duplicate retry is actor-attributed durably before returning the stored result
retrying the same command with a different audit-only reason returns the original state result, advances no generation, and records that retry separately
long-lived tombstones do not retain recoverable low-entropy operator reasons or require unsafe key retention

candidates.approach: Keep a minimal PostgreSQL command tombstone indefinitely, separately from the one-year actor/reason audit, containing only an opaque random command ID, keyed canonical-request MAC plus key ID, action, result code, latch epoch, and expected/result generation; retain its verification keys and prohibit removal/rollback.

Use a gate-minted immutable, signed request envelope whose opaque command ID binds the canonical request and expiry; deliver the envelope before execution and reject expired envelopes before any store lookup, then delete command-result rows after the maximum retry horizon while preserving one-year actor/reason audit.

prototype_questions.question: Which permit and identity-validation contract lets application instances reject forged, cross-instance, stale, and replayed permits while safely stopping new handlers within the accepted five-second limit during gate-service loss?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted design separates workload PAUSE from individual-operator RESUME and uses short-lived generation-bound permits. Issuer/audience validation, instance identity binding, signing-key rotation, and local handler-start validation must be testable without allowing a public ecommerce identity or caller-chosen instance ID to control the global gate.
decision_criteria: workload identity can PAUSE but cannot RESUME
only individually authenticated operators with the dedicated role can RESUME
permit binds verified subject to deployment, instance incarnation, leader, latch, and gate generations
permit binds an unpredictable signed request nonce to its outstanding issuance request
registration and drain proof bind a unique authenticated instance to a broker-observed connection, not caller-supplied identifiers
forged, stale, cross-instance, and replayed permits reject
lost gate connectivity stops new handler starts by the conservative five-second expiry

candidates.approach: Use a gate-issued signed short-lived permit with an epoch-scoped signing key, authenticated workload identity binding, strict issuer/audience/algorithm/expiry checks, and current leader-epoch bootstrap before admission.

Use an opaque one-use permit bound to an authenticated instance registration and require an online gate-service admission check at each handler start, failing closed whenever the gate service cannot be reached.
